core.h: Malthus and the concept of struggle for existence
core.p: Reading Thomas Malthus's "An Essay on the Principle of Population" (1798) in 1838 gave Darwin the crucial insight: populations produce far more offspring than can survive, leading to a constant struggle for limited resources. This struggle means individuals with advantageous variations are more likely to survive and reproduce.
bullets: Malthus: human populations grow geometrically, food arithmetically.
Darwin applied this to all organisms.
Result: "struggle for existence" — competition for food, mates, space.
Favourable variations increase reproductive success.

callouts.p: The competition among individuals of a population for limited resources, leading to differential survival and reproduction.
Quote Malthus by name and year (1798) when explaining the origin of the struggle concept.

core.h: Darwin's private development of the theory (1838‑1858)
core.p: After the Malthus insight, Darwin drafted a 35‑page "sketch" (1842) and a 230‑page "essay" (1844) but withheld publication, fearing scientific and religious backlash. He continued gathering evidence — barnacle taxonomy, plant breeding experiments, correspondence with breeders — to make his case airtight.
bullets: 1842: 35‑page sketch (not published).
1844: 230‑page essay, shared only with close friends (Hooker, Lyell).
1846‑1854: eight‑year barnacle monograph — established credibility as a taxonomist.
Conducted pigeon breeding to demonstrate artificial selection parallels.
Corresponded with Asa Gray, Thomas Henry Huxley, and others.

callouts.p: Darwin's delay meant Wallace's 1858 letter forced a joint announcement.
Do not state Darwin published before 1858; his first public presentation was the joint Linnean Society paper.

core.p: Wallace, a field naturalist in the Amazon (1848‑1852) and Malay Archipelago (1854‑1862), also read Malthus and recognized that environmental pressures shape species. In 1858, while ill with malaria on Ternate, he wrote an essay "On the Tendency of Varieties to Depart Indefinitely from the Original Type" and sent it to Darwin.
bullets: Collected > 125,000 specimens in Malay Archipelago.
Identified the "Wallace Line" — faunal boundary between Asian and Australian regions.
Essay posted 1858, reached Darwin June 1858.
Emphasised environmental change as driver of selection more than Darwin.

callouts.p: A biogeographical boundary separating the ecozones of Asia and Wallacea/Australasia, identified by Wallace.
Mention Wallace's malaria episode — it adds narrative detail examiners like.

core.h: The 1858 joint presentation to the Linnean Society
core.p: On 1 July 1858, Charles Lyell and Joseph Hooker arranged for Darwin's 1844 essay excerpt and Wallace's 1858 paper to be read together at the Linnean Society of London. The meeting was poorly attended and the papers received little immediate notice, but they established priority for both men.
bullets: Date: 1 July 1858.
Presenters: Lyell and Hooker (Darwin and Wallace absent).
Title: "On the Tendency of Species to form Varieties; and on the Perpetuation of Varieties and Species by Natural Means of Selection".
Both men acknowledged each other's independent work.
No immediate controversy; scientific community largely unaware.

callouts.p: The joint paper is the first public announcement of natural selection.
Do not confuse the 1858 Linnean Society reading with the 1859 publication of Origin.

core.h: Publication of "On the Origin of Species" (1859)
core.p: Darwin condensed his massive manuscript into a 502‑page book published 24 November 1859. The first edition sold out on the first day. It presented a comprehensive argument: variation exists, overproduction leads to struggle, natural selection preserves favourable variations, and over geological time this produces new species. The book deliberately avoided human evolution, addressing it later in "The Descent of Man" (1871).
bullets: Full title: "On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life".
Six editions in Darwin's lifetime, each revised.
Key chapters: Variation under domestication, Variation under nature, Struggle for existence, Natural selection, Laws of variation, Difficulties on theory.
Avoided explicit discussion of human origins.
Immediate impact: intense debate, support from Huxley, opposition from religious figures.

callouts.p: The preservation of favourable variations and the rejection of injurious variations, leading to adaptation and speciation over time.
Know the full title and the year 1859; examiners often ask for the publication date.

core.h: Core principles of natural selection (Darwin & Wallace)
core.p: Both naturalists agreed on five essential components: (1) Variation — individuals differ in heritable traits; (2) Overproduction — more offspring are produced than can survive; (3) Struggle for existence — competition for limited resources; (4) Differential survival and reproduction — individuals with advantageous traits leave more offspring; (5) Inheritance — advantageous traits are passed to the next generation. Over many generations this leads to adaptation and speciation.
bullets: Variation: raw material (genetic, though they didn't know genes).
Overproduction: exponential potential vs carrying capacity.
Struggle: intraspecific and interspecific competition, predation, disease.
Differential survival: "survival of the fittest" (phrase coined by Herbert Spencer, adopted by Darwin).
Inheritance: assumed blending inheritance (later corrected by Mendel).

head: Principle
Darwin's emphasis
Wallace's emphasis
rows: Similar, but more open to particulate ideas

callouts.p: Phrase coined by Herbert Spencer (1864) after reading Darwin; Darwin adopted it in later editions of Origin.
Do not attribute the phrase "survival of the fittest" to Darwin originally.

core.h: Differences in emphasis between Darwin and Wallace
core.p: While the core mechanism was identical, Darwin amassed a vast body of evidence (barnacles, pigeons, plants, fossils) and argued for gradualism. Wallace placed greater weight on environmental pressures and biogeography, and later diverged on human evolution, invoking spiritual forces for the human mind. Darwin's "Origin" provided a comprehensive, evidence‑rich framework; Wallace's 1858 essay was concise and focused on the logical necessity of selection.
bullets: Darwin: extensive empirical support, gradual change, sexual selection.
Wallace: biogeography (Wallace Line), environmental determinism.
Human evolution: Darwin naturalistic; Wallace spiritualist for higher faculties.
Speciation: Darwin emphasised divergence via isolation; Wallace emphasised ecological separation.

callouts.p: Wallace later campaigned for spiritualism — not required for the exam but explains his later divergence.
If asked to compare, mention evidence base (Darwin) vs biogeography (Wallace).

core.p: Initial reaction mixed; Huxley championed it, while many scientists clung to blending inheritance. The rediscovery of Mendel's laws (1900) and the development of population genetics (Fisher, Haldane, Wright) in the 1920s‑30s created the Modern Synthesis, uniting natural selection with genetics. Today, natural selection remains the central explanatory mechanism in evolutionary biology, supported by DNA evidence, experimental evolution, and antibiotic resistance studies.
bullets: 1860 Oxford debate (Huxley vs Wilberforce) — public perception.
Early criticism: blending inheritance would dilute variation.
Mendel's particulate inheritance solved the dilution problem.
Modern Synthesis (1930s‑40s) integrated genetics, selection, drift, mutation.
Current evidence: genome sequencing, observed selection in real time (e.g., peppered moths, antibiotic resistance).

callouts.p: The mid‑20th‑century fusion of Darwinian natural selection with Mendelian genetics and population genetics.
Link B5.2f to B5.2e (antibiotic resistance) as modern evidence for natural selection.

analogy.p: Imagine a sieve shaking a mixture of different‑sized pebbles (variation). Only pebbles small enough to pass through the holes (environmental pressure) fall into the collector (survive and reproduce). Over many shakes, the collector becomes enriched in small pebbles. The analogy breaks down because pebbles do not reproduce or pass on their size; in biology, the survivors pass on heritable traits, and the "holes" (environment) can change over time.

terms.d: The differential survival and reproduction of individuals due to differences in heritable traits, leading to adaptation.
Differences in traits among individuals of a population; the raw material for selection.
The production of more offspring than can survive to maturity, creating competition.
Competition among individuals for limited resources such as food, mates, and space.
Individuals with advantageous traits survive and reproduce more successfully than others.
The transmission of heritable traits from parents to offspring.
Rapid diversification of a lineage into many forms, each adapted to a distinct niche.
A faunal boundary separating Asian and Australasian species, identified by Alfred Russel Wallace.
The geological principle that present‑day processes operated similarly in the past, implying an ancient Earth.
Populations grow geometrically while resources grow arithmetically, leading to inevitable competition.
An outdated model where parental traits mix irreversibly in offspring, later replaced by particulate (Mendelian) inheritance.
The integration of Darwinian natural selection with Mendelian genetics and population genetics in the 1930s‑40s.
The London learned society where Darwin and Wallace's joint paper was read on 1 July 1858.
The Royal Navy ship on which Darwin served as naturalist from 1831‑1836.
A group of closely related finch species on the Galápagos Islands showing beak adaptations to different diets.
Human‑directed breeding of plants and animals for desired traits; used by Darwin as an analogy for natural selection.
Phrase coined by Herbert Spencer (1864) describing natural selection; adopted by Darwin in later editions.

mistakes.w: Darwin invented the idea of evolution
mistakes.r: Darwin provided the mechanism (natural selection); evolution was discussed before him (e.g., Lamarck).

mistakes.w: Darwin published his theory immediately after the Beagle voyage
mistakes.r: He developed it privately from 1838, but only presented jointly with Wallace in 1858 and published Origin in 1859.

mistakes.w: Wallace stole Darwin's idea
mistakes.r: Wallace independently conceived natural selection; they communicated and agreed to joint publication.

mistakes.w: Natural selection means "survival of the strongest"
mistakes.r: It means differential reproductive success of heritable variants; "fittest" refers to reproductive output, not physical strength.

mistakes.w: Darwin knew about genes and DNA
mistakes.r: Darwin had no knowledge of genetics; he assumed blending inheritance, later corrected by Mendel.

mistakes.w: The 1858 Linnean Society meeting caused an immediate scientific revolution
mistakes.r: The meeting was poorly attended and the papers received little notice at the time.

mistakes.w: Darwin's finches were the only evidence he used
mistakes.r: He also used fossils, biogeography, embryology, domesticated animal breeding, and plant experiments.

mistakes.w: Wallace Line is a physical line on the ocean floor
mistakes.r: It is a biogeographical boundary based on species distributions, not a geological feature.

mistakes.w: Darwin's theory was fully accepted by all scientists by 1860
mistakes.r: Many scientists resisted, especially due to blending inheritance; acceptance grew after the Modern Synthesis.

mistakes.w: Natural selection acts on acquired characteristics
mistakes.r: It acts only on heritable (genetic) variation; acquired traits are not inherited.

exam.q: State two observations Darwin made on the Galápagos Islands that supported his idea of natural selection.
model: Finch beak shapes varied between islands and matched available food sources.
Giant tortoise shell shapes differed between islands with different vegetation.
exam.tip: Name the specific organisms (finches, tortoises) and the trait (beak, shell).

exam.q: Explain how reading Malthus's essay helped Darwin formulate natural selection.
model: Malthus described human populations growing faster than food supply.
Darwin realised all organisms produce more offspring than can survive.
This creates a struggle for existence where favourable variations are preserved.
exam.tip: Link Malthus → overproduction → struggle → selection.

exam.q: Describe the events leading to the joint presentation of Darwin and Wallace's papers in 1858.
model: Wallace sent Darwin an essay on natural selection in June 1858.
Darwin, urged by Lyell and Hooker, agreed to a joint reading.
Extracts from Darwin's 1844 essay and Wallace's 1858 paper were read at the Linnean Society on 1 July 1858.
Both men were credited as independent co‑discoverers.
exam.tip: Include names Lyell, Hooker, Linnean Society, and the date.

exam.q: Compare the evidence bases used by Darwin and Wallace to support natural selection.
model: Darwin drew on extensive data: barnacle taxonomy, pigeon breeding, plant experiments, fossils, biogeography.
Wallace relied mainly on biogeographical patterns (e.g., Wallace Line) and observations in the Malay Archipelago.
Darwin's evidence was broader and more experimental; Wallace's was more observational and geographic.
exam.tip: Use the terms "experimental" for Darwin and "biogeographical" for Wallace.

exam.q: Why did Darwin delay publishing his theory for over 20 years?
model: He feared scientific criticism and religious backlash.
He wanted to gather overwhelming evidence (barnacles, breeding experiments).
He was concerned about the problem of blending inheritance diluting variation.
exam.tip: Mention both social and scientific reasons.

exam.q: Outline the five main principles of natural selection as described by Darwin and Wallace.
model: Variation exists among individuals in a population.
Overproduction leads to more offspring than can survive.
Struggle for existence results from limited resources.
Differential survival and reproduction favour advantageous traits.
Advantageous traits are inherited by the next generation.
exam.tip: List them in logical order; use the exact phrasing "variation, overproduction, struggle, differential survival, inheritance".

exam.q: Explain how the Modern Synthesis resolved the problem of blending inheritance.
model: Mendel's particulate inheritance showed traits are inherited as discrete units (genes).
Population genetics (Fisher, Haldane, Wright) demonstrated how allele frequencies change under selection.
This provided a genetic mechanism that prevents dilution of variation.
Natural selection could now be mathematically modelled and integrated with genetics.
exam.tip: Name Mendel and the three population geneticists.

exam.q: Give one piece of modern evidence that supports natural selection, and explain why it is convincing.
model: Antibiotic resistance in bacteria: random mutation confers resistance; antibiotics kill non‑resistant cells; resistant bacteria survive and reproduce.
Observed in real time, with DNA sequencing confirming the genetic change.
Directly demonstrates variation, selection, and inheritance.
exam.tip: Link to B5.2e (antibiotic resistance) for synergy.

exam.q: What is the Wallace Line and why is it significant for biogeography?
model: A faunal boundary between Asian and Australasian species identified by Wallace.
It shows that species distributions reflect evolutionary history and geological separation.
exam.tip: Define it as a biogeographical, not geological, line.

exam.q: Describe the role of artificial selection in Darwin's argument for natural selection.
model: Darwin used pigeon and plant breeding to show humans can produce dramatic change in few generations.
He argued nature, acting over vast time, can produce even greater change.
Artificial selection provided a familiar analogy for the power of selection.
exam.tip: Mention pigeons specifically; they were Darwin's favourite example.

exam.q: Explain why the 1858 Linnean Society reading did not cause an immediate scientific revolution.
model: The meeting was poorly attended and the papers were read by proxies.
The scientific community was largely unaware; the impact came after Origin (1859).
exam.tip: Contrast the 1858 reading with the 1859 book publication.

worked.q: A student is asked: "Darwin and Wallace both proposed natural selection. State one similarity and one difference in how they developed their ideas." Provide a model answer worth 4 marks.
steps: Identify a similarity: both were influenced by Malthus's principle of population and recognised that overproduction leads to a struggle for existence.

Identify a difference: Darwin amassed a wide range of experimental and observational evidence over 20 years (barnacles, pigeons, fossils) before publishing, whereas Wallace formulated the idea during fieldwork in the Malay Archipelago and sent a concise essay to Darwin in 1858.
Structure the answer: first sentence similarity, second sentence difference, using comparative language.
Check that both points are clearly attributed to the correct naturalist.
worked.ans: Similarity: Both Darwin and Wallace independently applied Malthus's idea that populations overproduce, creating a struggle for existence that drives natural selection. Difference: Darwin spent over two decades gathering diverse evidence (barnacle taxonomy, pigeon breeding, fossil records) before publishing, while Wallace arrived at the same conclusion during his fieldwork in the Malay Archipelago and communicated it in a single 1858 essay.

worked.q: Calculate the approximate number of years between Darwin's return from the Beagle voyage and the publication of "On the Origin of Species".
steps: Beagle returned: 2 October 1836.
Origin published: 24 November 1859.
Subtract years: 1859 - 1836 = 23 years (plus ~2 months).

worked.q: A 6‑mark question: "Explain how the modern synthesis combined Darwin's natural selection with Mendelian genetics to overcome the problem of blending inheritance." Provide a structured answer.
steps: State the problem: blending inheritance would halve variation each generation, making selection ineffective.
Introduce Mendel: particulate inheritance — traits are discrete units (genes) that do not blend.
Explain population genetics: Fisher, Haldane, Wright showed how allele frequencies change under selection, drift, mutation.
Conclude: The Modern Synthesis (1930s‑40s) unified natural selection with genetics, providing a mathematical framework and restoring variation as a permanent resource for selection.
worked.ans: Blending inheritance would dilute variation each generation, undermining natural selection. Mendel's particulate inheritance showed traits are passed as discrete genes that retain their identity. Population geneticists (Fisher, Haldane, Wright) mathematically demonstrated how allele frequencies shift under selection, drift, and mutation. The Modern Synthesis merged these insights, giving natural selection a robust genetic mechanism and solving the dilution problem.
